title: Illegal charges on public nursing-home residents and the Travers report (2005)
description: For decades medical-card holders in public long-stay care had charges deducted from their pensions under 1976 regulations; in October 2004 the Attorney General advised the Government that the charges had no legal basis. A report by former Forfás chief executive John Travers, brought to Cabinet by Health Minister Mary Harney in March 2005, criticised officials of the Department of Health over almost three decades and found, according to the Irish Examiner, that the issue had never been brought to Martin's attention in an appropriate manner while he was Minister for Health (2000–2004). Opposition parties questioned how much he knew: the Irish Examiner reported that a 2001 Ombudsman report had warned the charges were unconstitutional and that a constituent's 2001 letter on the matter had been acknowledged by his office. Martin's spokeswoman said he had repeatedly told the Dáil the charges were levied under the 1976 regulations and was not aware of a problem until the Attorney General's advice; he said the Dáil had not exercised its accountability role effectively in the 1990s.
key_facts: Repayments were expected to go to more than 300,000 people, their families and estates, at a cost the Irish Examiner put at up to €2 billion
The Travers report found no documentary evidence that Martin had been properly briefed
No finding of wrongdoing was made against Martin

title: Dismissal of Agriculture Minister Barry Cowen (July 2020)
description: Barry Cowen, the Fianna Fáil TD Martin appointed Minister for Agriculture when his government took office on 27 June 2020, faced questions within days over a 2016 drink-driving ban, for which he apologised in the Dáil on 7 July. New reports then said the Garda record of the incident suggested he might have tried to avoid a checkpoint, which Cowen denied. On 14 July Martin backed Cowen in the Dáil in the afternoon, after seeing the Garda record for the first time that morning; that evening he announced that, on his advice, the President had terminated Cowen's appointment, because Cowen would not make a further statement or answer questions in the Dáil, which Martin called 'simply untenable'. Cowen said he was 'surprised and disappointed' and that the decision had 'undermined and potentially prejudiced my entitlement to fair process'.
key_facts: Cowen was dismissed a little over two weeks after his appointment; the Irish Times called it virtually unprecedented
Martin briefly took the agriculture portfolio himself before appointing Dara Calleary

title: Oireachtas Golf Society dinner ('Golfgate') and the resignation of Dara Calleary (August 2020)
description: On 19 August 2020, the day after Martin's government tightened COVID-19 limits on indoor gatherings, about 80 people, including Agriculture Minister and Fianna Fáil deputy leader Dara Calleary, EU Trade Commissioner Phil Hogan and Supreme Court judge Séamus Woulfe, attended an Oireachtas Golf Society dinner in Clifden, Co Galway. Calleary resigned on 21 August; Martin said there would 'not be one rule for those in office' and that he understood the public anger. After further details of Hogan's movements emerged, Martin publicly suggested that he 'reconsider his position'; Hogan resigned as Commissioner on 26 August. Four organisers, including independent TD Noel Grealish and former Fianna Fáil senator Donie Cassidy, were prosecuted for breaching the regulations; on 3 February 2022 Galway District Court dismissed the charges against all four, the judge finding that the organisers had done everything to comply. Martin was not a party to these proceedings.
key_facts: Calleary was the second agriculture minister to leave Martin's cabinet in under two months
Judge Mary Fahy: 'I'm satisfied the organisers did everything to comply'

title: Robert Troy's undeclared property interests and resignation as Minister of State (2022)
description: Robert Troy, a Fianna Fáil Minister of State in Martin's government, resigned on 24 August 2022 after reports that he had not fully declared his property interests in the Dáil register; he called the omissions 'genuine errors and human errors'. Government sources told the Irish Times that Martin had not sought the resignation; Martin accepted it 'with regret', saying Troy had 'made serious errors' in his declarations and had apologised. In December 2024 the Standards in Public Office Commission found that Troy had contravened the Ethics Act 'on multiple occasions, in some respects inadvertently and in some respects negligently', but had acted in good faith. Troy is again a Minister of State in Martin's second government. Martin was not the subject of the investigation.
key_facts: Troy told RTÉ he owned or part-owned 11 properties
SIPO found 'this pattern of omissions or errors in successive declarations was a serious matter'
The Irish Times describes Troy as a Minister of State in October 2026

title: Neutrality: the 2023 security policy forum and the removal of the triple lock
description: As Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs and Defence, Martin organised the Consultative Forum on International Security Policy, held in Cork, Galway and Dublin in June 2023 and chaired by Professor Louise Richardson. President Michael D. Higgins criticised the forum in a Business Post interview, and People Before Profit TD Richard Boyd Barrett called it a 'ready-up' for closer alignment with NATO; Higgins later apologised for a remark about Richardson's DBE. Martin defended the forum, saying it was not a 'binary choice' between neutrality and NATO membership. In 2026 his second government introduced the Defence (Amendment) Bill to remove the requirement for UN approval of deployments; the opposition accused the Government of betraying neutrality and demanded a referendum, and recalled that Martin had previously described the triple lock as 'at the heart of Ireland's neutrality'. Martin says the reform 'in no way' undermines military neutrality.
key_facts: The Bill passed second stage 79–71 on 21 October 2026 after a debate guillotined at under four hours
Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald called it 'a profound betrayal'; Martin called her remarks 'outrageously hyperbolic'

title: Israel's closure of its Dublin embassy and accusations of antisemitism (2024–2025)
description: On 15 December 2024 Israel announced it would close its embassy in Dublin over what Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar called the Irish government's 'extreme anti-Israel policies', citing Ireland's recognition of Palestine and its decision, approved by the Cabinet on 11 December 2024 on Martin's proposal as Minister for Foreign Affairs, to join South Africa's genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice; Sa'ar also called Taoiseach Simon Harris an 'antisemite'. Martin rejected the claim that Ireland was hostile to Israel, saying it was holding Israel to account over the war in Gaza. In March 2025, after reports that Israel's ambassador to the United States had called him 'an antisemite', Martin said the assertions were 'false' and that he 'utterly' rejected them, pointing to his visit to Israel after the 7 October 2023 attack and his calls for the release of hostages.
key_facts: Martin said there were no plans to close Ireland's embassy in Israel
Ireland recognised the State of Palestine on 28 May 2024

title: Speaking-rights dispute over the government's independent supporters, including Michael Lowry (2025)
description: On 22 January 2025 the Dáil failed to nominate Martin as Taoiseach after the Ceann Comhairle, Verona Murphy, suspended the sitting several times amid opposition protests against plans to give opposition speaking time to four Regional Independent TDs, led by Michael Lowry, who had agreed to support the government. The Moriarty Tribunal had found in 2011 that Lowry had an 'insidious and pervasive influence' on the bidding process for the second mobile phone licence when he was a Fine Gael minister in the 1990s. Martin called the disruption a 'subversion of the Irish Constitution' by a 'premeditated, coordinated and choreographed' opposition, and said there had been 'no deal whatsoever' on speaking rights in the coalition talks; Sinn Féin said Lowry could not 'masquerade' as an opposition TD. The Dáil nominated Martin the next day, after it was agreed that the group would not be given opposition speaking time as an interim measure. The Government then said it would propose standing-order changes giving the group time during Leaders' Questions; after a motion amending the standing orders was debated on 25 March 2025, the Dáil has had a separate 'Other Members' Questions' slot after Leaders' Questions, in which Martin answers questions.
key_facts: Martin: 'the first time, I think, in over 100 years, that the Dáil has failed to elect a government'
Martin's Oireachtas page lists his answers in 'Other Members' Questions' (Ceisteanna ó na Comhaltaí Eile), for example on 21 October 2026

title: Fianna Fáil's 2025 presidential campaign: Jim Gavin's withdrawal and criticism of Martin's leadership
description: Martin backed Jim Gavin, a former Air Corps officer, Dublin Gaelic football manager and Irish Aviation Authority executive, as Fianna Fáil's presidential candidate; former Taoiseach Bertie Ahern, who had considered standing, said he could not run without the leadership's support and that Martin was 'anti-me'. Gavin beat MEP Billy Kelleher 41–29 in the parliamentary party vote on 9 September 2025. On 5 October Gavin withdrew from the campaign after questions about €3,300 in rent overpaid by a former tenant and not returned; his name stayed on the ballot. Martin called the decision 'the correct one' and said the party had asked Gavin repeatedly about tenant issues. Independent TD Catherine Connolly, nominated by Oireachtas members of Sinn Féin, Labour, the Social Democrats and other opposition groups, won on 24 October with 63.4% of valid votes; Gavin received 7.2%. Veteran TDs Willie O'Dea, Seán Ó Fearghaíl and Pat 'the Cope' Gallagher demanded publication of the party's internal review; Martin called some media coverage 'selective and inaccurate' and said calls for him to quit were nothing new.
key_facts: Connolly's 914,143 votes were the most first preferences ever won by a candidate in Ireland, according to Wikipedia
Fianna Fáil's review of the campaign was published in December 2025

title: Handling of the April 2026 fuel protests
description: From 7 April 2026, as fuel prices rose during the war involving Iran, hauliers and agricultural contractors held convoys and then blockaded roads, Dublin's O'Connell Street and fuel depots, including the State's only oil refinery at Whitegate, Co Cork. Martin said the protests were 'wrong' and 'not a legitimate form of protest', called the refinery blockade 'an act of national sabotage', and said the Government would deal only with representative bodies such as the Irish Road Haulage Association. After the government agreed a support package of about €500 million, independent Minister of State Michael Healy-Rae resigned, saying 'the leader of the country should have listened'. Three of Fianna Fáil's youngest TDs and veteran TDs Willie O'Dea and Seán Ó Fearghaíl criticised the party leadership, and TheJournal reported a short-lived attempt at a leadership challenge. Martin said his leadership was not under threat and later described many protesters as 'genuine people' under pressure.
key_facts: Martin and Tánaiste Simon Harris condemned the depot blockades; Harris called them 'sinister'
Senior Fianna Fáil figures seen as possible successors publicly backed Martin
